newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin breaks taboo, announces heart surgery.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin breaks taboo, announces heart surgery.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, breaking a taboo observed by generations of Kremlin leaders, admitted to Russians on Thursday in a television interview he was in poor health and had agreed to heart surgery.

Yeltsin's announcement came at the start of a new four-year term, as Russia grapples with economic problems and the aftermath of war in Chechnya. In a land where poor health has traditionally meant waning political power it was a bold step.
As if to demonstrate he remained in control, Yeltsin used the interview to make a major policy statement on Chechyna, backing a peace deal forged by his security chief.
"I want to have a society based on truth here, that means no longer hiding what we used to hide," said the 65-year-old Russian leader, who had two heart attacks last year.
Doctors had told him they had discovered heart problems and advised him to have an operation or cut back his workload.
"Passive work has never suited me. Nor can it suit me now. That's why an operation and full recovery, as they promise, is better for me than passive activity, passive work," he added, talking slowly.
Yeltsin disappeared from public view in late June. His aides said he was simply tired and recovering from a vigorous election campaign that brought him victory over a communist rival.
Since then, Yeltsin has made only one public appearance, on August 9, briefly showing up at his inauguration ceremony.
In Soviet times, leaders' health was considered a secret and the state often went to bizarre lengths to hide problems.

When hardline communist chief Leonid Brezhnev was in his decline, pictures were falsified and events specially staged for television to suggest he was well. For months before his successor Yuri Andropov died, officials said he had a cold.
In recent months Yeltsin's health had been shrouded in a secrecy reminiscent of old times.
Yeltsin is due to meet visiting German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Saturday.

A top Kremlin aide, Dmitry Ryurikov, told a news briefing earlier on Thursday that Yeltsin would meet Kohl in the Rus hunting lodge outside Moscow where he is now vacationing. He said the meeting was due to last about four hours.
Yeltsin's long absence and his apparent distraction from the day-to-day management sparked media speculation about who was running Russia.
Many fingers have pointed at Yeltsin's boyish chief-of-staff, Anatoly Chubais, 41, rather than his formal "number two", Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, 58.
"The feeling is growing by the day that Boris Yeltsin...has left Anatoly Chubais in control and not Viktor Chernomyrdin," the liberal newspaper Sevodnya wrote.
Yeltsin's administration for its part has done everything to try to demonstrate that the president was in charge and that he was aware of problems the country faced.
Yeltsin said he backed his government's statement condemning U.S. air strikes against Iraq.

The government said on Wednesday that U.S. strikes were an "inappropriate" reaction to Baghdad's military operation in its northern region, and demanded that all military actions threatening Iraq's sovereignty be stopped.
Yeltsin said he will discuss Iraq with Kohl.

Another Kremlin strongman, Yeltsin's security tsar Alexander Lebed, was in Chechnya on Thursday, going over with separatist leaders measures to build on a shaky truce and political deal aimed at ending the 21-month war in the southern region.

Lebed said after talks with rebel chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov that more Russian-separatist joint patrols would be sent in and new provisional bodies set up to maintain order in the battle-scarred regional capital Grozny.
Lebed said that he and Maskhadov had agreed to make Grozny a demilitarised zone in which only the members of the joint patrols would be allowed to carry guns.

Maskhadov and Lebed, whom Yeltsin dispatched less than a month ago to end the Chechen war, struck a ceasefire deal two weeks ago and later agreed to defer a decision on the most sensitive issue of the conflict, Chechnya's independence.
The rebels view Chechnya as a separate state. Moscow says the region must stay part of the vast Russian Federation.

They agreed a fortnight ago that troops and rebels would leave Grozny, the scene of worst fighting since the start of conflict in late 1994 when Russia sent troops to quell Chechnya's independence bid.
Yeltsin said he had backed Lebed's peace deals except for the part providing for an early withdrawal of Russian troops.
"I think we should not be in a hurry to do that. The rest I have backed and fully approved," Yeltsin said.
